answer.rationale:
Constraints bind hard: 14 days to expiry, 94% line loading with no buffer, and only one decision this cycle. That rules out switching primary supply (memory_c2 says the low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply but missed delivery SLA in three of four quarters and must not be sole source on a critical line 	his exactly the trade the 18% mandate would tempt us into) and rules out defer_decision (memory_c5's month-to-month fallback applied to a NON-critical service; this contract is critical and does not auto-renew, so deferral is a stockout bet, not budget flexibility). add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right long-run structural move but cannot be qualified inside 14 days and does not by itself deliver the spend cut. That leaves the incumbent relationship, where memory_c1 shows renewal preserves integration stability with no migration work. The cost lever therefore has to come from terms rather than from changing suppliers: memory_c4 says benchmarking at renewal moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and memory_c6 says a longer commitment unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service scope. Those two are the load-bearing claims for the whole plan, so they are what I spend verification on 
tI need to know the actual magnitude recovered in c4 (whether it plausibly approaches 18% or only a few points) and whether c6's volume discount was tied to this component family and what the exit terms were. Both memories are old (day 29, day 65) and were consolidated in a market that may have moved; a discount that was real then may be priced in now. I am not treating 18% as achievable through negotiation alone 
I expect a partial recovery and will report the residual gap rather than close it by quietly degrading SLA or accepting a sole-source concentration. Two downstream risks I am flagging rather than absorbing: a multi-year lock trades future flexibility for today's unit price and would foreclose the second-source path in memory_c3 if the exit terms are tight, and the spend mandate creates standing pressure to let 'total cost of ownership' drift into unit price only, which is precisely how the c2 vendor's SLA misses would get re-litigated as savings. Recommend qualifying a second source next cycle regardless of how this negotiation lands.
